result:
Solution A is correct and Solution B is not.

**Solution B is wrong.** Its formula gives $k(3,3)=1$, but $P(x)=-(x^3-x)^3$ has $[x^3]P=1$. Since $m^3-m$ is divisible by $3$ for every integer $m$, $P(m)$ is divisible by $3^3$, so $k(3,3)\ge 3$. More generally, $-(x^p-x)^n$ always gives $k(n,p)\ge n$, but B gives $k(11,11)=1$, which violates this bound.

**Solution A checks out.** Write $P=\sum_j b_j (x)_j$ with $b_j\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ holds automatically, and $p^k\mid P(m)$ for all $m$ is equivalent to $v_p(b_j)+v_p(j!)\ge k$ for all $j$. The condition $[x^n]P=1$ becomes $\sum_j b_j s(j,n)=1$.

- **Upper bound:** Modulo $p$, $(x)_{pm+r}\equiv (x^p-x)^m(x)_r$. Counting degrees shows that $p\mid s(j,n)$ for every $j>pn$, and $s(pn,n)\equiv(-1)^n\not\equiv0 \pmod p$. Since $v_p(j!)$ is nondecreasing, any $k$ with $k>v_p((pn)!)$ requires some $j>pn$ with $p\nmid s(j,n)$, which doesn't exist. So $k(n,p)\le v_p((pn)!)$.
- **Achievability:** With $k=v_p((pn)!)$, the $j=pn$ term has coefficient a unit mod $p$ and no divisibility constraint. The $j=n$ term has $s(n,n)=1$ with a factor $p^{k-v_p(n!)}$, so the ideal generated by the coefficients is all of $\mathbb{Z}$.

Hence $k(n,p)=v_p((pn)!)=n+v_p(n!)$.

**Recomputing the sum:**
- $p=11$: $v_{11}(n!)=1$ for $n=11,\dots,15$, so $k=12,13,14,15,16$, summing to $70$.
- $p=13$: $v_{13}(n!)=0$ for $n=11,12$ and $1$ for $n=13,14,15$, so $k=11,12,14,15,16$, summing to $68$.

Total $=70+68=138$, matching Solution A.

WINNER: A
